Contact Us English Português Español English Português Español The latest from Marvin Compliance The Margin Is Leaking in Your Compliance File A missing origin document can now stop a shipment at the border or turn a profitable cargo into a loss. For companies in bio-economy trading, the trade escrow determines whether the transaction can be executed and whether it gains a positive margin. The old playbook doesn't survive contact with today's trade environment Supply chains used to run on static quarterly forecasts and low-cost sourcing logic. That model assumed a level of stability that no longer exists. Three forces are breaking it: Regulatory fragmentation: A wave of evidence-based requirements now sits on top of physical trade, and each one demands something different: EUDR — traceability from the exact plot of land to the shelf, or the shipment doesn't clear the border CBAM — embedded carbon, priced into the shipment at the border SAF mandates — certified feedstock, without which the fuel doesn't qualify at all CSDDD — value-chain due diligence, stacked on top of the above National laws , like Germany's LkSG and France's duty of vigilance, each adding their own version of the same ask Different levers — market access, tariff, eligibility, corporate liability — but each one turns unverified origin data into a direct balance-sheet liability. For a forestry, agribusiness, or bio-feedstock exporter, weak provenance on a single shipment is enough to get it turned back at the border. Volatile tax and duty frameworks: Tariffs shift by region, transfer-pricing rules get more intricate, and import/export tax regimes change faster than legacy batch-tracking systems can keep up. Brazilian paper exports show how fast: a 25% US tariff took effect in mid-2025, and exports fell 48.5% in the first half of 2026 as buyers moved to Canadian and Asian suppliers. Brazil's own tax reform is adding another layer on the same timeline, replacing five overlapping taxes with a dual VAT that companies now have to run in parallel with the old system. Meanwhile, the new EU-Mercosur and EU-India trade deals cut tariffs on most goods traded, but only for shipments backed by a self-certified statement of origin. By the time any of this shows up in a delivered quote, the buyer has already moved on. Geopolitical and freight instability: Suez, Panama, and the Strait of Hormuz can each reprice a shipment overnight. In March 2026, conflict around the Strait of Hormuz drove the sharpest single-month oil price move on record — Brent crude rose roughly 65% in a few weeks. Container rates swung just as hard: the Shanghai freight index rose 149% in 2024 during the worst of the Red Sea rerouting, fell back 37% by mid-2025 as capacity normalized, then jumped another 35% into early 2026 as Hormuz tensions hit. Breakbulk rates, driven by renewable energy and heavy-project cargo, are up 20% since 2025 on a separate track entirely. ‍ Put together, these forces put origin and compliance data on the same footing as cost and price: an input that decides whether the shipment is profitable at all. How the gap closes Maintaining Freedom to Operate now requires managing compliance across three tiers simultaneously, not sequentially — the four tiers forward-thinking organizations are already building around: Entity-level controls — dynamic verification of supplier tax standing, regional compliance status, and real-time sanction checks. Product-level provenance — verifiable batch passports and Molecular Twins that prove feedstock origin, carbon footprint, and regulatory alignment down to the transaction, including across mass-balance blending points where physical and certified volumes diverge. Automated dynamic compliance — the legal, environmental, and financial documentation that clears customs and releases finance flows, executed without manual bottlenecks. Landed cost simulation — modeling tariffs, taxes, and freight across alternative routes and suppliers before a shipment moves, catching cost swings before they show up in the landed cost. Any one of these layers alone is incomplete. Entity checks without product-level provenance leave gaps that a single bad batch can expose. Provenance without automated documentation just becomes another silo of unused data. The organizations pulling ahead are synchronizing all three on one ledger, which is what turns compliance from a defensive function into an operational one. What followed was the transformation of traceability from a fragmented process into an efficient operational infrastructure. ABOUT SUZANO Suzano is the world’s largest pulp manufacturer, one of the largest paper producers, generating $9 billion in annual revenue. With over 100 years of history as a Brazilian multinational, Suzano is core to the bioeconomy, producing sustainable and renewable products from eucalyptus. What makes Suzano unique is its largely integrated model: the company grows most of its own trees with third-party wood filling the rest, operates its own mills, and manages its own global trade - controlling every layer of the supply chain from forest to final customer. Guided by the principle that life renews itself, Suzano integrates sustainability into every part of its operations, from forest management to industrial processes and global trade, delivering innovative solutions while maintaining operational excellence at a global scale. ‍ Operating at the Edge of Complexity With $9.1 billion in annual net revenue flowing through a supply chain of over 14,000 export shipments per year spanning 70+ countries, even minor compliance lapses carried significant operational, financial, and reputational consequences. THE EUDR CHALLENGE As EUDR implementation approached, the stakes became uniquely acute for Suzano. The EU Deforestation Regulation requires operators to prove the legal and deforestation-free origin of raw materials at every stage of the fiber supply chain - not just at the point of export, but traced back to the specific plot of land where each tree was grown. For most companies, this is difficult. For a fully integrated operator like Suzano - managing 2.9 million hectares of forest assets, running its own mills, and handling its own global trade - the supply chain spans three distinct operational layers, each with its own systems, documentation, and stakeholders. The information required was distributed across multiple internal systems, supplier networks, and documentation repositories, resulting in a highly manual, time-consuming process that required ongoing coordination among teams, suppliers, and stakeholders. Under EUDR rules, if even a single tier of the fiber supply chain lacks verified origin data, the downstream operator cannot complete a valid Due Diligence Statement. For a global exporter such as Suzano, a single missing data point could disrupt the movement of multi-million-dollar shipments into the EU market. ‍ ‍ The Solution: Cross-Border Supply Chain Traceability with Automated Compliance Shield Suzano partnered with Marvin to deploy a centralized Track & Trace platform built around six integrated modules. Together, they connect land intelligence, certification workflows, product traceability, supplier risk management, stakeholder transparency, and trade planning into a single auditable system of record. Crucially, the platform was designed to follow Suzano’s fully integrated structure - spanning all three operational layers of the business. At the forest level, it monitors land eligibility and deforestation risk in real time. At the manufacturing level, it maps each production batch back to its verified origin. At the trade level, it generates the documentation and certifications required by customers and regulators in over 100 countries. Marvin’s AI data-orchestration engine automatically ingests, maps, and validates supply chain data across all three layers, reducing manual processes and centralizing compliance information into a single source of truth.
